source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ κατακολουθήσας Ἀκουσιλάῳ γράφει·
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Now, Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, who was called Pleistonices, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he was disposed in a rather hostile manner towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and having even written a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, the king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become king in the place of Argive Inachus, dug up Auaria, as Ptolemy of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. Now, this Ptolemy was a priest, and having set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books, he says that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it is inferred that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. Of these, the Attic, which are from Cecrops, the two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger; and the Arcadic, which are from Pelasgus, are nine; and this one is also said to be autochthonous. And of these, the Phthiotic, which are from Deucalion, are younger by two. And into the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are reckoned from Inachus, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the things of the Assyrians are much older than the Greek things, as Ctesias says, it will be shown that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian rule, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the movement of Moses out of Egypt, during the reign of Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive, occurred. Now, in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who was after Inachus, there was the flood that occurred during the time of Ogygus, and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the Cretan in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man to be born; whence also the poet of the Phoroneis says that he was the father of mortal men. From this, Plato, following Acusilaus, writes in the Timaeus;
pass_b_english: We will examine shortly the fact that the philosophers' doctrines appeared among the Hebrews, but first, as the proper order requires, we must discuss the times of Moses. Through that discussion it will be demonstrated conclusively that Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his *Against the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first book of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless, our own account also obliges us to run through the relevant chronological statements. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Pleistonices, addresses them in the fourth book of his *Egyptian History*. Although he is an Egyptian by birth and displays a decided hostility toward the Hebrews—going so far as to compose a treatise against the Jews—he still cites Amosis, the Egyptian king, and the events of his reign, and he calls Ptolemy of Mendes as his witness. Ptolemy's words run as follows: "Amosis, who became king in the time of the Argive Inachus, laid waste Avaris," as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemy was a priest who set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three complete books, and he states that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses. From this it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

The most ancient of the Greek traditions are the Argolic, that is, those traced from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. Compared with these, the Attic traditions deriving from Cecrops—the two‑natured, autochthonous figure, to use Tatian's exact phrase—are forty generations younger; the Arcadic traditions from Pelasgus, who is also said to be autochthonous, are nine generations younger; and the Phthiotic traditions from Deucalion are younger by two generations. By the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are counted from Inachus, amounting, so to speak, to four hundred years. If, as Ctesias asserts, Assyrian history is far older than the Greek, then the exodus of Moses from Egypt under the Egyptian Amosis and the Argive Inachus falls in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire and the thirty‑second year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus. Meanwhile in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who succeeded Inachus, occurred the flood of Ogygus and the early Sicyonian kingdom—first Aegialeus, then Europs, then Telchin—along with the Cretan dynasty in Crete. review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex chronological arguments and historical citations. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering that preserves all nuances of the Greek text, including the specific generational counts and the distinction between the Assyrian and Greek timelines. All citations (Tatian, Cassian, Apion, Ptolemy of Mendes, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Ctesias, Acusilaus, and Plato) are correctly handled.
